title: Wi-Fi Dead Zones
statement: An office floor plan is a grid of strings. `#` is a wall, `.` is open floor, and `R` is a router standing on open floor.
A router's signal travels up, down, left, and right through open floor, never through walls, and reaches every cell within `range` steps. Return how many open floor cells (`.`) no router reaches.

examples.explanation: The two middle cells of the bottom row are 3 steps from both routers.
The wall blocks the only path to the last cell.

constraints: every row has the same length

hints: Running a separate search from every router repeats a lot of work. Could all the routers spread at the same time?
Put every router in one queue at distance 0 and run a single breadth-first search that never goes past range.
Mark a cell visited when you add it to the queue, then count the '.' cells that were never visited.
pitfalls: Running one BFS per router, which multiplies the work by the number of routers.
Using DFS, which doesn't find shortest distances, so it gets range wrong.
Counting router cells as dead zones.
Marking cells visited when they leave the queue instead of when they enter it, which adds duplicates.
interviewerNotes: Look for the multi-source BFS idea. Ask why it gives each cell its distance to the nearest router.
Ask why DFS doesn't work for a distance limit.
Check range = 0 and a grid with no routers.
Follow-up: signal can pass through walls at a cost of 3 steps. That needs Dijkstra or a 0-1 BFS.
